opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The title was deliberately provocative, and I'll own that. I wasn't saying humans have no role in labeling data. I was challenging an assumption that's been baked into how most teams approach computer vision for the last decade or so: that the first step on any project is to go out and get a massive pile of human annotations, as many bounding boxes and polygons as you can afford.

That made sense in the ImageNet era. But the ground has shifted. We now have foundation models, vision-language models, and zero-shot detectors that can generate pretty reasonable labels automatically, for a tiny fraction of the cost and time of human labeling. In a lot of the experiments we ran, models trained on auto-generated labels came surprisingly close to models trained on human labels. Sometimes the gap was small enough that it's hard to justify spending all that money and time on manual annotation up front.

So the real challenge was to the workflow and the mindset. Instead of annotation as a giant upfront tax, I think the human effort should go where it's actually valuable: curating the data, understanding failure modes, verifying and correcting the cases where the automatic labels break down, and building really good evaluation sets. Human judgment is still critical, but it should be targeted rather than brute force. Annotation as we knew it, the "label everything by hand" approach, is what I'd say is dead, or at least should be.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the claim does not mean humans have no role in labeling data.

r002.rationale: It challenges the practice of collecting a massive pile of annotations upfront and calls the “label everything by hand” approach dead.

r003.rationale: It says foundation models and related systems can generate reasonable labels automatically, with human effort focused on cases where those labels fail.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the title was intentionally provocative, I'll admit that up front. What I was really trying to challenge is this assumption that's been baked into computer vision and machine learning for the better part of two decades, which is that the path to a better model runs through more labeled data. More boxes, more polygons, more segmentation masks, more humans sitting in front of screens clicking on things.

And look, that recipe worked. ImageNet, COCO, all of that, it got us here. But I think we've reached a point where the economics and the epistemics of it have both broken down. The economics are obvious. If you're a company trying to deploy a model in a real environment, you're spending enormous amounts of money and time on annotation, and a huge fraction of that effort is wasted. You're labeling frames that look like ten thousand other frames you already labeled. You're not learning anything new from them.

The epistemic problem is more subtle, and that's the one I actually care about more. The annotation itself is treated as ground truth, as this clean signal. But anyone who has run an annotation project knows it's not. Two annotators disagree constantly. The taxonomy you picked at the start of the project turns out to be wrong six months in. The label encodes the annotator's biases and the project manager's shortcuts. So we've built this whole field on a foundation that we pretend is bedrock and is really more like sand.

So what I was pushing on in the post is a shift in where the human effort goes. Instead of humans labeling data and models consuming the labels, I think the more productive framing is that the human's job is to understand the data. What's in it, where the gaps are, where the model is confused and why, which examples actually matter. Foundation models and self-supervised approaches have gotten good enough that they can handle a lot of the grunt labeling. The scarce resource now isn't labels, it's judgment about the data.

And I'll say, I got some pushback on it, which was the point. People said, well, you still need some labels. Of course you do. "Dead" was rhetorical. But the mindset of annotation as the central activity, as the thing you scale, I do think that's over. Or it should be.

r001.rationale: The response says that some labels are still needed and that “Dead” was rhetorical.

r002.rationale: It describes redundant frames being labeled as wasted effort and says treating annotation as the activity to scale is over.

r003.rationale: It says foundation models and self-supervised approaches can handle much of the routine “grunt labeling”.

astra-6.text: I was trying to challenge the assumption that building a computer vision system has to start with people manually labeling huge amounts of data. We’ve come to treat that as a prerequisite: collect images, draw boxes or masks, and then train a model. But the labels aren’t really the objective—the objective is a system that understands what we need it to do. So the provocation was: can we rethink how people teach these systems, using their expertise to guide and correct them rather than asking them to annotate everything?

r001.rationale: The response questions annotating everything and proposes human guidance, but it does not clearly say annotated data will still be needed.

r002.rationale: It identifies asking people to annotate everything as the practice to rethink, which conveys that labeling all data cannot remain the approach.

r003.rationale: It does not mention foundation models or say they can replace human labeling in routine cases.

sol-6.1.text: I was trying to challenge the assumption that, to build a computer vision system, you first need to collect a huge dataset and pay people to annotate all of it. The title was deliberately provocative. I wasn’t saying that human input has no value; I was questioning whether drawing boxes and labeling images at scale should remain the default way we provide that input. Can we build systems that learn more from the data itself and ask people for help where their knowledge is most useful?

r001.rationale: The response says human input still has value, but it does not clearly state that annotated data will continue to be needed.

r002.rationale: It questions the practice of collecting a huge dataset and paying people to annotate all of it, and challenges large scale labeling as the default.

r003.rationale: It does not mention foundation models or say they can replace human labeling in routine cases.
